title: Can I Bear to See My Friends' Faces Fall?
translation_notes: Fresh T1 translation made directly from the Batch 003 pinned Tamil after completed P0/source review. No pre-existing English translation was consulted.
Historically derogatory caste speech is retained only inside attributed quotation because it is the causal evidence in Kalaignar's explanation of the troupe's failure; it is not narrator endorsement.
Three documented page joins are reconstructed continuously.
paragraphs: The man who had bought my play Palaniyappan for one hundred rupees approached me after starting an arts troupe called the Dravidian Actors' Association, with the plan of staging plays that would propagate the movement's ideas. I agreed. The troupe first set up camp in Villupuram. They also asked me to join the company and act. I agreed on one condition: I would act only in plays I had written.

Before the performances began, rehearsals were held for a month in Villupuram. A house was rented for the members of the troupe. Thennan and C. D. Moorthy were with me. From childhood I had never been accustomed to being alone. One would usually find me with two or three friends.

There are some people who do not understand the meaning of affection or friendship; merely seeing a man with four friends is enough to make them jealous and prompt malicious talk. I was never one to worry because somebody's eyes were irritated by the sight. I could not bear to watch my friends' faces fall.

Among my many friends, one or two may have thought the affection I showed was madness; or they may have used it and deceived me. In the same way, things may have happened without my knowledge—through people in between—that made them think wrongly of me. But one must not build a whole new philosophy about friendship itself out of a few incidents. With Thennan and Moorthy beside me, I faced the pains of Villupuram.

Let me briefly describe our daily routine there. After waking and finishing our morning duties, everyone came to the central hall. We had to stand in a row. The chorus song customary in theatre companies was not an invocation to God. It was a salutation to the land. We sang a national song beginning "Dravidam, Dravidam." After that came a meagre breakfast, and then rehearsals.

When rehearsal ended we set out to bathe. Bathing was a major problem there. We had to go at least a mile from the house where we stayed. Our baths were at places where water was piped into the fields. Yes—that pipe water was our Courtallam waterfall. It would be quite true to say that in those one or two minutes I found some coolness in life. Yet only I knew that even then the drops bursting from my eyes mixed with the water from the pipe.

After bathing we started back home under a fierce sun. With a small towel tied around my waist, my washed shirt drying over my shoulder, I held above my head like an umbrella the dhoti I had whitened with a half-anna bar of washing soap, letting it dry as I walked. Once home, after the clothes dried, we put them on and performed penance waiting for the afternoon meal.

After enduring that "punishment" we would close our eyes for a while. Do you imagine I could sleep? I had taken on family responsibility while still young and was suffering inwardly, unable to bear the load. My only consolation was that our work was useful in spreading party principles through drama. Rehearsal began again at four in the evening. We finished dinner by eight and left for the theatre shed to put on our stage makeup.

We had to sing the chorus at every meal and then again at the beginning and end of the play—a total of five times a day. Somehow the day's play would begin. Why do I stress the word "somehow"? To make clear the fact that whether the play began at all depended on the day's collection.

For the first week we staged Palaniyappan, which I had written. The theatre owner suggested that, to attract people, the play might be called either Santa or Palaniyappan. Whatever name we gave it, people did not come. Those who saw it praised it. But there was no collection. The theatre company began falling into debt. What could we do when the day's collection was eighty rupees, or seventy?

One day Periyar came to preside over the play. Another day Anna came. I can never forget the incident when the owner of the theatre company asked Anna himself for a loan of ten rupees, Anna smiled and gave him the ten rupees, and, before leaving town after the performance, patted me on the back and said with affection, "Karuna, I am going now."

There was one important reason our plays failed to bring successful collections in Villupuram. The people there hated the name "Dravidian Actors' Association." Why? For political reasons? No! No! I reproduce the contemptuous caste talk heard in the bazaar:
"A theatre company has come from Nagapattinam, brother. There are more than forty boys. They're all educated Pariah fellows. They've even named the company after the Pariah caste."
"Is that so? Then only people of that caste should go and see the play."

That was the reason for our failure. It is an example of how high caste hatred raised its head in towns such as Villupuram twenty-five years ago. It is also evidence that people had not yet gained the maturity to understand the truth that "Dravida" was the name of an ancient people of the South, without caste distinction. In Villupuram in 1944, the word "Dravida" was misunderstood and, because of that, fine people from the oppressed communities were spoken of with contempt.

Yet four years earlier, at the Justice Party conference held in Tiruvarur in 1940 under Periyar's leadership, Mr. P. Balasubramaniam had moved the resolution "Dravida Nadu for the Dravidians," and Arignar Anna and C. Basudev had seconded it. Scholars such as the missionary Caldwell had concluded from their research that Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu and other languages arose from one ancient Dravidian language, and that those who spoke them were Dravidians.

On that basis, at the Tiruvarur conference, Arignar Anna delivered a long explanatory speech about the paths to the artistic, cultural and economic advancement of the Dravidians. K. A. P. Viswanatham of Tiruchirappalli, who until then had been General Secretary of the Justice Party, resigned from that position after differences with party leader Periyar on various matters. Anna, then assistant editor of the newspaper Viduthalai, was elected General Secretary of the Justice Party.

To awaken enthusiasm in the country for the words "Dravida" and "Dravidian," Anna began the weekly Dravida Nadu from Kanchipuram. Alongside it he created in Kanchipuram an auxiliary body of sorts under the name Dravidar Kazhagam. No one then expected that this auxiliary organization would one day become a movement spreading across the country.

As General Secretary of the Justice Party, Anna longed to find a way for the party to grow, gain new speed and acquire a new goal. The great leaders in the Justice Party were lovers of luxury—mansions, jasmine-covered beds, towers, drums and pomp. The huts and the voices rising from them had little chance of reaching their ears. Anna tried to free the Justice Party from the grip of such people.

It was in the same year, 1944, when I was staging plays in Villupuram, that the Justice Party conference was held in Salem. The grandees and notables of the Justice Party tried to remove Periyar from the party leadership. To prevent that and protect Periyar's leadership, Anna made a whirlwind tour across the country and increased support among party workers.

To break the opposition, to realize his aim of taking the Justice Party into the homes of the poor, and to express his indestructible attachment to Indian freedom, Anna brought a resolution at the Salem conference. That historic resolution came to be known as the Annadurai Resolution.

Anna's resolution proclaimed that the name Justice Party should be changed to Dravidar Kazhagam; that titles such as "Sir," "Rao Bahadur" and "Diwan Bahadur" bestowed by British rule should be renounced; that those holding honorary-magistrate and nominated posts should resign them; and that people should discard caste names attached to their personal names.

The resolution was subjected to thirty-five hours of debate. The party's scrutiny committee opposed it fiercely. Later, at the public conference, speeches were made both supporting and opposing it, and finally Anna gave his explanation. Party comrades and members of the public welcomed it with eager applause. Seeing this, the great men of the Justice Party left the conference one after another. At last the Annadurai Resolution passed amid thunderous applause.

Anna not only protected Periyar's leadership; he also gave the Justice Party a new turn. And it was that very word "Dravida," then beginning to spread, that became a problem for us in Villupuram, damaged the collections of our theatre company, and finally made us pack our bags and leave that town.
